sukkah-2b-14-14.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalled that Queen Helene had a sukka in Lod more than twenty cubits high, and the Elders went in and out of it without saying a word to her about it. The other Sages answered that this proves nothing: she was a woman, and women are exempt from the sukka. Rabbi Yehuda replied that she had seven sons, and moreover that she did everything only as the Sages directed.
sukkah-2b-14-14.why: A teaching holds that a sukka taller than twenty cubits is unfit, while Rabbi Yehuda allows one up to forty or fifty; the Gemara raises his precedent as an objection to how two later Sages explained that dispute.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who allows a very tall sukka and cites Queen Helene's sukka as proof.

people.name: Queen Helene
people.about: A queen whose sukka in Lod was over twenty cubits high; Rabbi Yehuda says she had seven sons and followed the Sages in everything.

terms.meaning: The temporary booth Jews live and eat in during the festival of Sukkot. Its size and height are set by law.
An ancient measure of length, roughly the length of a forearm, about half a meter.
The leading Sages of the time, whose silence Rabbi Yehuda takes as approval.

sukkah-10b-2-2.note: Minyamin, Rav Ashi's servant, got his shirt wet and spread it over the sukka to dry. Rav Ashi told him to take it down, so that people would not say they were roofing the sukka with something that can become ritually impure. Minyamin objected that anyone could see it was wet and only drying. Rav Ashi answered that he meant: take it down once it is dry.
sukkah-10b-2-2.why: The discussion is about decorations and cloths placed on or under a sukka's roofing, and Rav Ashi has just ruled on decorations spread at its sides; this incident shows his concern for how a cloth on the roof looks to onlookers.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: Rav Ashi's servant, who spread his wet shirt on the sukka to dry.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Minyamin's master, who told him to take the shirt down.

terms.meaning: The sukka's roof must be made of plant material that grew from the ground and is not a finished object; a garment cannot serve as roofing.
In Jewish law, finished vessels and garments can become ritually impure; anything that can is unfit to roof a sukka.

sukkah-10b-4-4.note: Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna came to the house of the Exilarch, where Rav Nahman put them up in a sukka whose decorations hung four handbreadths below the roofing. They kept silent and said nothing. Rav Nahman asked them whether the Sages had taken back their ruling. They answered that they were on a mission for a mitzva, and so were exempt from the sukka altogether.
sukkah-10b-4-4.why: Rav Nahman had ruled that such a sukka is fit, while Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna ruled it unfit; the story shows that their silence while staying in it was not a concession.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who held that a sukka with decorations four handbreadths below the roof is unfit.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Rav Hisda's companion, who shared his view.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: In charge of the Exilarch's household, by the translation's account; he held such a sukka fit and lodged the two in it.

terms.meaning: The official head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who kept a large household.
A measure of about the width of a palm, roughly 8 to 10 centimeters.

terms.term: On a mission for a mitzva
terms.meaning: Someone traveling to perform a religious duty is exempt from other duties, such as dwelling in a sukka, while doing so.

sukkah-14b-8-8.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalled a time of danger when he and others brought boards four handbreadths wide, roofed a porch with them and sat beneath them. The other Sages answered that this proves nothing, since what people do in a time of danger is no proof.
sukkah-14b-8-8.why: Rav and Shmuel disagree about which boards Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda were arguing over; this teaching, in which Rabbi Yehuda cites boards four handbreadths wide, supports Rav's version of their dispute.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who allows boards four handbreadths wide as sukka roofing and recalls using them himself.

terms.meaning: A period of persecution. The translation explains that non-Jewish rulers had forbidden building a sukka, so it was disguised as an ordinary porch roof.
A measure of about the width of a palm, roughly 8 to 10 centimeters.

sukkah-16b-5-7.note: Rav Dimi, arriving from the Land of Israel, reported an incident from Tzippori: once people forgot to bring a Torah scroll to the synagogue before Shabbat began. The next day they found sheets already spread over posts along the way, used them as partitions, carried the scroll and read from it. The Gemara corrects the wording: they cannot have spread the sheets on Shabbat itself, so they must have found them already in place.
sukkah-16b-5-7.why: The Gemara has argued that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei each accept hanging partitions only in limited cases, neither for Shabbat carrying; so it asks whose view Tzippori followed, and answers Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage on whose authority, the Gemara says, the people of Tzippori acted.

terms.meaning: Jewish law forbids carrying objects on Shabbat in open areas unless they are enclosed by partitions, which is why the sheets mattered.
A wall that hangs from above without reaching the ground, like a sheet on posts. The Sages dispute when it counts as a real wall.

sukkah-20a-10-10.note: Reish Lakish said: I am the atonement for Rabbi Ḥiyya and his sons. When the Torah was forgotten in the Land of Israel, Ezra came up from Babylonia and reestablished it; when it was forgotten again, Hillel the Babylonian came up and reestablished it; when it was forgotten yet again, Rabbi Ḥiyya and his sons came up and reestablished it. He then cites their ruling: Rabbi Dosa and the Rabbis agreed that the mats of Usha can become ritually impure and those of Tiberias cannot, and disagreed only about mats from other places.
sukkah-20a-10-10.why: The Gemara is asking what the word ḥotzalot means. Reish Lakish says it means plain mats, and this tribute introduces the teaching of Rabbi Ḥiyya and his sons on which that view rests.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage who honors Rabbi Ḥiyya and his sons and cites their ruling

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Came up from Babylonia with his sons and restored forgotten Torah

people.name: Ezra
people.about: Came up from Babylonia and restored the forgotten Torah

people.name: Hillel the Babylonian
people.about: Came up from Babylonia and restored the forgotten Torah

people.name: Rabbi Dosa
people.about: Sage whose dispute with the Rabbis about mats is explained

terms.meaning: An expression of deep devotion and respect for someone.
A state, under Torah law, that bars a person or object from holy use; some objects can take it on and others cannot.
Two towns: the text says Usha's mats were made for lying on and Tiberias' mats for partitions and roofing.

sukkah-20b-6-6.note: Rabbi Hananya recalled that when he went down to Babylonia, he met an Elder who told him that one may roof a sukka with a mat. When he came back to his uncle, Rabbi Yehoshua, and told him, Rabbi Yehoshua agreed. Rav Hisda added that this holds only for a mat without an upturned edge.
sukkah-20b-6-6.why: The discussion is whether various mats count as vessels that can become ritually impure, which would make them unfit as sukka roofing; this report allows a mat, and Rav Hisda limits it to one that is not a vessel.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya
people.about: The nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua, who heard the ruling from an Elder in Babylonia.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Rabbi Hananya's father's brother, who agreed with the Elder's ruling.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A later Sage who limits the ruling to mats without an upturned edge.

terms.meaning: Babylonia, home of the largest Jewish community outside the Land of Israel.
A raised rim that turns a flat mat into a container, which can become ritually impure and so cannot roof a sukka.

sukkah-21b-7-7.note: Rabbi Shimon recalled an incident involving Tavi, the slave of Rabban Gamliel, who slept under a bed in the sukka. By the translation's account, Rabban Gamliel remarked that Tavi did so because he was a Torah scholar and knew that slaves are exempt from the sukka. Rabbi Shimon said that from Rabban Gamliel's conversation they learned two things: that slaves are exempt from the sukka, and that one who sleeps under a bed in the sukka has not fulfilled his obligation.
sukkah-21b-7-7.why: The mishna disputes whether sleeping under a bed inside a sukka counts; Rabbi Yehuda says it does, and Rabbi Shimon cites Tavi's case to show it does not, since a bed is like a tent that blocks the roofing.

people.name: Tavi
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's slave, who slept under a bed in the sukka.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Tavi's master, whose remark about him taught two laws.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident and what it teaches.

terms.meaning: A non-Jewish slave in a Jewish household, who keeps only some commandments and is exempt from the sukka.
Properly performed the commandment, here dwelling under the sukka's roof.

sukkah-23a-2-2.note: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva were traveling together on a ship, and Rabbi Akiva built a sukka on the deck. The next day the wind blew and tore it away. Rabban Gamliel said to him: 'Akiva, where is your sukka?' The text does not give Rabbi Akiva's reply.
sukkah-23a-2-2.why: Rabban Gamliel rules a sukka on a ship unfit and Rabbi Akiva rules it fit; the mishna follows Rabbi Akiva, and Abaye explains they disagree over whether a sukka must withstand a sea wind.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's traveling companion, who held a sukka on a ship unfit.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Built a sukka on the ship, holding it fit.

terms.meaning: The temporary booth Jews live and eat in during the festival of Sukkot.

sukkah-27a-0-1.note: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai was brought a cooked dish to taste, and Rabban Gamliel was brought two dates and a bucket of water, and each said: take them up to the sukka. But when Rabbi Tzadok was given less than an egg-bulk of food, he took it in a cloth, ate it outside the sukka, and did not say a blessing after it.
sukkah-27a-0-1.why: The previous mishna allows a snack outside the sukka, so the Gemara asks why this one tells a story that seems to contradict it; it answers that one may choose to be strict, then weighs Rabbi Tzadok's case against Rav Yosef and Abaye.

people.name: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Brought a cooked dish to taste, he insists on eating it in the sukka

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Brought two dates and water, he insists on having them in the sukka

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Eats a small amount outside the sukka without a blessing afterward

terms.meaning: The booth in which Jews eat during the festival of Sukkot.
A measure of food the size of an egg; less than that is treated here as too little to require a sukka, hand-washing or a blessing afterward.

sukkah-27b-7-7.note: Rabbi Elai went to greet his teacher, Rabbi Eliezer, in Lod on the Festival. Rabbi Eliezer said to him: 'Elai, you are not one of those who rest on the Festival.' For Rabbi Eliezer used to say: 'I praise the lazy, who do not leave their houses on the Festival,' since it is written, 'You shall rejoice, you and your household.'
sukkah-27b-7-7.why: The Gemara sets this against Rabbi Yitzhak's teaching that one must greet one's teacher on a Festival, and reconciles them: the duty applies when one can go and return the same day, and Rabbi Eliezer's objection when one cannot.

people.name: Rabbi Elai
people.about: A student who went to greet his teacher on the Festival.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Rabbi Elai's teacher in Lod, who held that people should stay home on the Festival.

terms.meaning: One of the pilgrimage holidays, here Sukkot, when people traditionally rejoiced at home with their families.
The translation explains this word in the verse as one's wife; one who is away cannot rejoice with her.

sukkah-27b-9-10.note: Rabbi Eliezer was staying in the Upper Galilee in the sukka of Yohanan son of Rabbi Elai when the sun began to shine into the sukka. Yohanan asked whether he might spread a sheet over it, and Rabbi Eliezer answered only that every tribe of Israel produced a judge. When the sun reached the middle of the sukka he asked again, and Rabbi Eliezer said every tribe produced prophets, and Judah and Benjamin set up kings by prophets' word. When the sun reached Rabbi Eliezer's feet, Yohanan spread a sheet, and Rabbi Eliezer threw his cloak over his shoulder and left. The Gemara comments that he never said anything he had not heard from his teacher.
sukkah-27b-9-10.why: One of several stories about Rabbi Eliezer on Sukkot; the Gemara then asks how he could stay in someone else's sukka, given his own rulings, and concludes it was Shabbat and Yohanan's question was about building on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The guest who would not answer a question he had not heard ruled on by his teacher.

people.name: Yohanan, son of Rabbi Elai
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's host, who asked whether he could spread a sheet against the sun.

terms.term: Spreading a sheet over the sukka
terms.meaning: Adding a cover to a structure; the question is whether this counts as forbidden building or as adding to a temporary tent.
The hilly northern part of the Land of Israel.

sukkah-28a-1-2.note: While Rabbi Eliezer stayed in the Upper Galilee, people asked him thirty laws about the sukka. To twelve he answered that he had heard a ruling, and to eighteen that he had not; Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says it was the reverse. They asked whether everything he said came only from what he had heard. He answered that they had now forced him to say something he had not heard from his teachers: no one ever came into the study hall before him, he never slept there, never left anyone behind there, never engaged in idle talk, and never said anything he had not heard from his teacher.
sukkah-28a-1-2.why: The previous story ended with the Gemara saying Rabbi Eliezer never said anything he had not heard from his teacher; this similar incident shows that habit in his own words.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage asked thirty questions about the sukka, who answered only what he had heard from his teachers.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Gives the reverse count: eighteen heard and twelve not.

terms.meaning: Rules of Jewish law; here, questions about the laws of the sukka.
The house of study where Sages and students learned Torah together.

sukkah-28b-6-6.note: When the daughter-in-law of Shammai the Elder gave birth, Shammai broke away the plaster of the roof, leaving the beams, and roofed over the bed so that the newborn would be under a sukka roof.
sukkah-28b-6-6.why: The mishna exempts small children who still need their mother; the Gemara asks whether the incident contradicts this, and answers that the mishna is incomplete: Shammai was strict even for infants, and this is an example.

people.name: Shammai the Elder
people.about: The Sage who roofed over his newborn grandchild's bed.

terms.meaning: A child below the age of religious obligation. The mishna obligates only a child who no longer needs his mother in the sukka.
The layer of plaster over the roof beams; with it removed, the beams could serve as sukka roofing.

sukkah-29a-3-3.note: Abaye was sitting before Rav Yosef in the sukka when the wind blew and brought splinters down from the roofing. Rav Yosef told the household to clear his things out of there. Abaye objected that the mishna says one leaves only when rain would spoil a congealed dish. Rav Yosef answered that for him, since he is delicate, this was as bad as a spoiled congealed dish.
sukkah-29a-3-3.why: The mishna says one may leave the sukka in rain hard enough to spoil a congealed dish; Rav Yosef's reply shows the measure depends on the person, so discomfort that bothers a delicate person counts.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rav Yosef's student, who questioned him for leaving the sukka.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who called himself delicate and left the sukka when splinters fell.

terms.meaning: A thick porridge that even a little rain ruins; the mishna uses it to measure when rain is heavy enough to leave the sukka.

sukkah-30a-2-2.note: Rabbi Yohanan, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, explained the verse 'For I the Lord love justice, I hate robbery in a burnt-offering' with a parable. A human king passing a customs house told his servants to pay the tax to the tax collectors. They asked: doesn't all the tax belong to you? He answered that all travelers would learn from him and not evade the tax. So too, God says He hates robbery in a burnt-offering, so that His children will learn from Him and keep away from robbery.
sukkah-30a-2-2.why: The Gemara has ruled that a stolen animal cannot be offered, even once it legally belongs to the robber, since a mitzva may not be done by means of a sin; this teaching on a verse about robbery and offerings follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who reports this teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: The Sage in whose name the teaching is given.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who in the parable's lesson hates robbery so His children will learn from Him.

terms.meaning: A Temple sacrifice burned entirely on the altar.
A toll station where travelers paid tax on goods passing through.

sukkah-31a-7-7.note: An old woman came before Rav Nahman and said that the Exilarch and all the Sages of his house were sitting in a stolen sukka. The translation explains she claimed the Exilarch's servants had stolen her wood to build it. She screamed, but Rav Nahman paid her no attention. She said: a woman whose father had three hundred and eighteen slaves is screaming before you, and you pay her no attention? Rav Nahman told the Sages that she was a screamer, and that she had a right only to the value of the wood.
sukkah-31a-7-7.why: The Gemara has just said that everyone agrees a person who builds a sukka from stolen wood owes the owner only the wood's value; Rav Nahman's ruling applies exactly that principle.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge before whom the old woman complained.

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, accused of sitting in a sukka made of her wood.

terms.meaning: The official head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
The number of servants Abraham led into battle in Genesis; the translation explains that she is claiming honor as a descendant of Abraham.

sukkah-36b-6-6.note: Rabbi Yosei recalled an incident in which Rabbi Akiva came to the synagogue with his etrog so large he carried it on his shoulder. Rabbi Yehuda answered: is that a proof? There too, the Sages told him, 'That is not beauty.'
sukkah-36b-6-6.why: The mishna disputes the maximum size of an etrog: Rabbi Yehuda says one must be able to hold two in one hand, while Rabbi Yosei allows one so large it needs both hands; Rabbi Yosei cites Rabbi Akiva's etrog as his proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who allows a very large etrog and tells the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Brought an etrog to the synagogue so large he carried it on his shoulder.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Disputes Rabbi Yosei, saying the Sages told Rabbi Akiva his etrog was not beautiful.

terms.meaning: A citron, a lemon-like fruit, one of the four species held on Sukkot.
The Torah calls the etrog the fruit of a beautiful tree, so an etrog that is not beautiful is unfit.

sukkah-37a-4-4.note: Rabbi Meir recalled that the prominent residents of Jerusalem used to bind their lulavs with gold rings. The Sages answered that this proves nothing: they bound them underneath with their own species.
sukkah-37a-4-4.why: The mishna disputes what may bind the lulav: Rabbi Yehuda says only its own species, Rabbi Meir says even a cord; Rabbi Meir offers Jerusalem's custom as proof, and the Sages explain the gold was only decoration.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage who allows binding the lulav with anything and cites the Jerusalem custom.

terms.meaning: A palm branch, held on Sukkot bound together with myrtle and willow branches.
Material from one of the four species of Sukkot, such as palm fibers, rather than an outside material.

sukkah-41b-5-5.note: Four leading Sages, Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva, were traveling together on a ship during the festival of Sukkot, and only Rabban Gamliel had a lulav, which he had bought for a thousand zuz. He used it to fulfill the mitzva and then gave it to Rabbi Yehoshua as a gift. Each Sage in turn used it and gave it to the next as a gift, and Rabbi Akiva, the last, returned it to Rabban Gamliel.
sukkah-41b-5-5.why: The mishna rules that on the first day of Sukkot one cannot use another person's lulav; the Gemara cites this voyage to show a lulav given as a full gift works. It also learns from the return that a gift given on condition of return still counts, and from the price how dear mitzvot were to them.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The only one on the ship with a lulav, bought for one thousand zuz; he passes it on as a gift and gets it back at the end.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Receives the lulav from Rabban Gamliel as a gift, uses it, and passes it on.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Receives the lulav from Rabbi Yehoshua, uses it, and gives it to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The last to use the lulav; he returns it to Rabban Gamliel.

terms.meaning: The palm branch (taken together with myrtle, willow and a citron) that the Torah commands Jews to take in hand on Sukkot.
The autumn Festival of Booths, a week-long holiday.
A silver coin; a thousand zuz was a very large sum.

sukkah-43b-11-12.note: One year the seventh day of Sukkot, the day of the willow branch, fell on Shabbat. Willow branches were brought before Shabbat and left in the Temple courtyard. The Boethusians, who rejected the Sages' view that this mitzva overrides Shabbat, found the branches and hid them under the stones, knowing the Sages would not let the stones be moved on Shabbat. The next day some ignorant people found the branches and pulled them out from under the stones, and the priests brought them and stood them at the sides of the altar.
sukkah-43b-11-12.why: Abaye brings this account against Rav Yosef, who held that the willow mitzva consists of standing branches beside the altar. The Gemara reads the ending as showing the willow was taken in hand and waved, and calls it a conclusive refutation of Rav Yosef.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who cites this account to challenge Rav Yosef.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage whose view about the willow branch Abaye is challenging.

terms.meaning: On Sukkot, willow branches were used in a Temple rite around the altar, with special emphasis on the seventh day.
A Jewish sect of the Temple period that disputed many rulings of the Sages, including this one.
A collection of early teachings from the same period as the mishna, organized like it.

sukkah-48b-11-11.note: During the Sukkot water-pouring ceremony at the altar, a Sadducee priest poured the water on his feet instead of on the altar. In anger, all the people pelted him with their etrogim. In the chaos a horn of the altar was damaged that day. They sealed the damaged spot with a fistful of salt, not because this made the altar fit for service, but so the altar would not be seen damaged; an altar missing a horn, a ramp, a base or its square shape is unfit for service.
sukkah-48b-11-11.why: The mishna says the priest pouring the water was told to raise his hand; the Gemara brings this incident next to that detail, as the event behind it.

people.name: Sadducee priest
people.about: An unnamed priest who poured the water on his feet rather than on the altar.

terms.meaning: On Sukkot, water was poured on the Temple altar alongside the usual wine offering.
Member of a Temple-era group that rejected many traditions of the Sages, including the water pouring.
The citron fruit carried with the lulav on Sukkot; plural etrogim.
A raised corner piece on each of the altar's four corners.

sukkah-51b-5-8.note: Rabbi Yehuda describes the great synagogue of Alexandria in Egypt: a vast basilica with a double colonnade, sometimes holding twice the number who left Egypt, with seventy-one golden chairs. It was so big that a sexton stood on a wooden platform and waved a scarf to signal when the people should answer amen. Craftsmen sat by trade, so a poor newcomer could find his fellow workers and get a living from them. Abaye said all of them were killed by Alexander of Macedonia. The Gemara says it was for settling in Egypt against the Torah's command; when Alexander arrived and found them reading a verse about a nation coming from afar like a swooping vulture, he took it as referring to himself, whose ship had arrived in half the expected time, and slaughtered them.
sukkah-51b-5-8.why: The Gemara has just quoted the Sages: whoever has not seen Jerusalem in its glory or Herod's Temple never saw a beautiful city or magnificent building. Rabbi Yehuda's saying about Alexandria is a parallel boast of that kind.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who describes the Alexandria synagogue.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who says all who gathered there were killed by Alexander.

people.name: Alexander of Macedonia
people.about: The conqueror who reads a Torah verse as a sign about himself and slaughters the community.

terms.meaning: The supreme court of seventy-one Sages; the synagogue's seventy-one golden chairs matched its members.
The synagogue attendant.
The response the congregation gives at the end of a blessing.

sukkah-52a-10-11.note: Abaye overheard a man telling a woman, Let us rise early and go on the road. Sure they meant to sin, he followed them for three parasangs through a marsh to stop them. They did nothing wrong, and as they parted he heard them say it had been a long way and pleasant company. Abaye said that had it been himself, he could not have held back, and he leaned on a doorpost in regret. An Elder came and taught him: anyone greater than another has a greater evil inclination.
sukkah-52a-10-11.why: The Gemara is reading Joel's verses as describing the evil inclination, and Abaye has just said it provokes Torah scholars more than anyone else; this incident illustrates his point.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who follows the couple and then realizes his own weakness.

people.name: a certain Elder
people.about: An unnamed older Sage who comforts Abaye.

terms.meaning: A Persian measure of distance, roughly three to four miles.
The Sages' term for the inner drive that pushes a person toward wrongdoing.

sukkah-56b-4-4.note: Miriam, daughter of a family in the priestly watch of Bilga, abandoned her faith and married a soldier in the army of the Greek kings. When the Greeks entered the Temple sanctuary, she kicked the altar with her sandal and said: Wolf, wolf, how long will you consume the property of the Jewish people while not standing by them when they are in trouble? When the Sages heard of it, they fixed the Bilga watch's ring in place and sealed its niche.
sukkah-56b-4-4.why: The mishna says the Bilga watch always divides the shewbread in the south, the side of the outgoing watch, even when arriving; this explains that penalty. The Gemara then asks why a whole watch should suffer for one daughter, and Abaye says a child repeats what she hears at home.

people.name: Miriam, the daughter of Bilga
people.about: Of the Bilga priestly watch; she abandoned her faith, married a Greek soldier, and kicked the altar.

people.name: Greeks
people.about: The army of the Greek kings, who entered the Temple sanctuary.

terms.meaning: One of the rotating groups of priests, each serving in the Temple for a week at a time.
Each watch had a ring for slaughtering its animals and a wall niche for its knives; fixing and sealing them barred Bilga from using its own.
The great altar in the Temple courtyard on which offerings were burned.

sukkah-56b-5-5.note: A second account of why the Bilga priestly watch was penalized: once its members were late arriving at the Temple. The watch of Yeshevav, Bilga's brother, came in with those who had arrived and served in the place of the missing members. As a result, Bilga always divides the shewbread in the south, while Yeshevav, his neighbor in the rotation, always divides it in the north. The Gemara remarks that although neighbors of the wicked do not usually profit, Bilga's neighbors did.
sukkah-56b-5-5.why: The mishna rules that the Bilga watch always divides the shewbread in the south; this is the alternative explanation to the story of Miriam. The Gemara then notes that on this account, penalizing the whole watch is easy to understand, since the whole watch was late.

people.name: Bilga
people.about: A priestly watch whose members were late to arrive at the Temple.

people.name: Yeshevav
people.about: Bilga's brother, the watch next to it in the rotation, which served in place of Bilga's absent members.

terms.meaning: Twelve loaves set out in the Temple each week and divided among the priests when the watches changed.
One of the rotating groups of priests, each serving in the Temple for a week; the incoming group divided in the north, the outgoing in the south.
